zh.q: 看不见摸不着，凭什么说通电导线周围有磁场？
zh.concl: 教材 A2.1 + A2.2 + A2.3：通电导线周围存在磁场（奥斯特 1820），磁场看不见但客观存在；铁屑在磁场里被磁化成一个个小磁针，轻敲玻璃板后沿磁感线排成链——所以能用它把磁场显示出来。
points: 奥斯特 1820：通电导线使小磁针偏转，第一次揭示电与磁的联系（教材 p.104–105）。
磁场客观存在、不用接触就起作用；铁屑在磁场里被磁化成小磁针，轻敲玻璃板后沿磁感线排成链（p.106 的演示手法）。
铁屑分布只是示意：真实演示要用很大的电流（或多匝线圈）才排得出来，本课读数一律按 2 A 计算；教材是先用条形磁体做对照、再换通电直导线，本课直接看三台通电导线。

zh.q: 直导线周围的磁感线是什么形状？
zh.concl: 教材 A2.7 原句：直线电流的磁感线是一圈圈的同心圆，这些同心圆都在跟导线垂直的平面上；磁感线首尾相接（闭合），纸面画出的只是这一族圆里的一个平面。
points: 同心圆，并且都在与导线垂直的平面上（教材 p.106 原句）。
不是从导线沿半径射出去——那是点电荷的电场（A7.2 的错法）。
纸面图只是三维这一族圆的一个截面，绕轴转一圈才看全。

zh.q: 电流方向一反过来，磁感线的方向怎么变？
zh.concl: 教材 A2.7 原句：用右手握住导线，让伸直的拇指所指的方向与电流方向一致，弯曲的四指所指的方向就是磁感线环绕的方向；改变电流的方向，各点的磁场方向都变成相反的方向。判据写成点积：B̂·(Î×r̂) 由 +1 变 −1。
points: 右手握导线：拇指沿电流、四指沿磁感线环绕方向。
电流反向 → 每一圈的绕向都反，而读数 20.0 μT 一点不变。
判据是 B̂·(Î×r̂)：反向前 +1、反向后 −1，不是「箭头掉头」那么简单。

zh.q: 离导线越远，磁场为什么越弱？
zh.concl: 教材 A2.4：磁感线密的地方磁场强、疏的地方弱；直导线的 B 与到导线的距离成反比（拓展口径），r 加倍 → B 减半。同一条读数还能和教材 p.110 的磁感应强度表对照：20 μT 只有地磁场平均值 50 μT 的 0.40 倍。
points: 疏密表示强弱：密处强、疏处弱（教材 p.106 原句）。
20 μT 只有地磁场平均值 50 μT（教材 p.110）的 0.40 倍，真实小磁针会被地磁场压住，所以本课用铁屑。

zh.q: 环形电流的磁感线从哪里穿进去、又从哪里绕回来？
zh.concl: 教材 A2.8 + 图 13.1-9：环形电流的磁感线是一族闭合曲线，从环的一侧穿出来、从另一侧绕回去；用另一种形式的安培定则——右手弯曲的四指沿电流环绕方向，伸直的拇指所指的方向就是轴线上磁场的方向（本课取 +x 端）。
points: 每条曲线都闭合：环内穿出、环外绕回。
整族曲线绕环轴转一圈才是全部，纸面只有一个子午面。
右手握线圈：四指沿电流、拇指沿轴线——和握导线时手指角色正好互换。

zh.q: 把一匝变成十匝，中间的磁场变几倍？
zh.concl: 教材 A4.5 原句「通电螺线管可以看作许多匝环形电流串联而成」：每一匝对中心的贡献同向叠加，所以 B 与匝数成正比（B₀ = μ0NI/(2R)，拓展口径），而磁感线的形状不变。
points: 多匝 = 串联的许多单匝，每一匝的贡献同向。
形状不变，只有疏密变——强弱变了、几何没变。

zh.q: 沿轴线往外走，磁场怎样变弱？
zh.concl: 轴线上处处 B̂ = n̂（同一方向，只是变弱）：B(z) = B₀/(1+(z/R)²)^{3/2}。z = R 时系数 0.354（25.13 → 8.89 μT），z = 2R 时只剩 0.089 倍。
points: 轴线上处处沿轴：方向不变、只是变弱。

zh.q: 螺线管内部为什么近似匀强？管口外又弱到多少？
zh.concl: 教材 A2.8 + A2.15 + 练习第 6 题：通电螺线管外部的磁场与条形磁体十分相似，内部近似匀强（磁感线是间隔相等的平行直线）；内部磁感线由 S 极指向 N 极，所以拇指方向（+x 端）就是 N 极。管口只剩一半的环在贡献，约为内部的一半（0.51）。
points: 内部近似匀强：磁感线平行、间隔相等（教材第 2 节的匀强磁场判据）。
中心 8128 μT、管口 4156 μT（0.51 倍）、管外 10.0 cm 只剩 248 μT。
内部磁感线由 S 极指向 N 极，拇指方向（+x 端）就是 N 极——外部与条形磁体十分相似。

zh.q: 考核：在螺线管上找到读数正好是内部一半的位置
zh.concl: 考核没有新结论：半值位置就是管口——「内部匀强、管口一半、外部像条形磁体」三件事在同一台装置上合体；判强弱一律回到磁感线疏密（教材练习第 6 题）。
points: 先把电流定在 2.0 A：B ∝ I，电流一变基准就变。
中心读数 8128 μT 的一半是 4156 μT。
读数降到一半时 z = 6.0 cm——正好是管口，再往外就迅速衰减。

en.q: It can't be seen or touched, so how do we know a current-carrying wire has a magnetic field around it?
en.concl: Textbook A2.1 + A2.2 + A2.3: a current-carrying wire has a magnetic field around it (Oersted 1820); the field is invisible but real; iron filings in the field are magnetized into tiny compass needles and, when the glass plate is tapped, line up in chains along the field lines, so they can make the field visible.
points: Oersted 1820: a current-carrying wire deflects a compass needle, the first link found between electricity and magnetism (textbook pp.104–105).
The magnetic field is real and acts without contact; iron filings are magnetized into small needles and, after the plate is tapped, line up along the field lines (the demonstration method on p.106).

The filing pattern is only illustrative: a real demonstration needs a very large current (or a multi-turn coil) to form it, while this lesson computes every reading at 2 A; the textbook first uses a bar magnet as a comparison and then a current-carrying straight wire, while this lesson goes straight to three current-carrying setups.

en.q: What shape are the field lines around a straight wire?
en.concl: Textbook A2.7: the field lines of a straight current are concentric circles, all in planes perpendicular to the wire; field lines close on themselves, and a drawing on paper shows only one plane of this family of circles.
points: Concentric circles, all in planes perpendicular to the wire (textbook p.106).
They don't radiate out from the wire along radii; that's the electric field of a point charge (the error in A7.2).
A drawing on paper is only one cross-section of this 3D family of circles; go all the way around the axis to see all of it.

en.q: If the current reverses, how does the direction of the field lines change?
en.concl: Textbook A2.7: grip the wire with your right hand with the extended thumb along the current, and the curled fingers point in the direction the field lines circle; reverse the current and the field at every point reverses. As a dot product: B̂·(Î×r̂) goes from +1 to −1.
points: Right hand grips the wire: thumb along the current, fingers in the direction the field lines circle.
Reverse the current → every circle reverses direction, while the 20.0 μT reading doesn't change at all.
The test is B̂·(Î×r̂): +1 before reversal, −1 after; it's more than "the arrows turn around".

en.q: Why is the field weaker farther from the wire?
en.concl: Textbook A2.4: the field is strong where field lines are dense and weak where they are sparse; for a straight wire B is inversely proportional to the distance from the wire (extension level), so doubling r halves B. The same reading can be compared with the field-strength table on textbook p.110: 20 μT is only 0.40 times the average Earth field of 50 μT.
points: Density shows strength: strong where dense, weak where sparse (textbook p.106).
r from 2.0 to 4.0 cm, B from 20.0 to 10.0 μT: it halves, not quarters.
20 μT is only 0.40 times the average Earth field of 50 μT (textbook p.110); a real compass needle would be dominated by Earth's field, so this lesson uses iron filings.

en.q: Where do the field lines of a circular current pass through, and where do they loop back?
en.concl: Textbook A2.8 + Fig. 13.1-9: the field lines of a circular current are a family of closed curves, emerging from one side of the loop and looping back to the other; use the other form of Ampère's rule: curl the fingers of the right hand along the current, and the extended thumb points along the field on the axis (the +x end in this lesson).
points: Every curve is closed: out through the loop, back around the outside.
The whole family of curves takes a full turn around the loop's axis; the page shows only one meridian plane.
Right hand grips the coil: fingers along the current, thumb along the axis, exactly swapping the roles from gripping a wire.

en.q: Turn one loop into ten: how many times stronger is the field in the middle?
en.concl: Textbook A4.5: "a current-carrying solenoid can be seen as many turns of circular current in series"; each turn's contribution at the center adds in the same direction, so B is proportional to the number of turns (B₀ = μ0NI/(2R), extension level), while the shape of the field lines stays the same.
points: Many turns = many single turns in series, each contributing in the same direction.
Shape unchanged, only density changes: the strength changed, the geometry didn't.

en.q: Moving out along the axis, how does the field weaken?
en.concl: On the axis B̂ = n̂ everywhere (same direction, just weaker): B(z) = B₀/(1+(z/R)²)^{3/2}. At z = R the factor is 0.354 (25.13 → 8.89 μT), at z = 2R only 0.089.
points: Along the axis everywhere: direction unchanged, just weaker.
Only 0.089 times at z = 2R (2.25 μT).

en.q: Why is the field inside a solenoid nearly uniform, and how weak is it outside the end?
en.concl: Textbook A2.8 + A2.15 + Exercise 6: outside, a current-carrying solenoid's field closely resembles a bar magnet's, and inside it is nearly uniform (field lines are evenly spaced parallel lines); inside, field lines run from S to N, so the thumb direction (+x end) is the N pole. At the end only half the coil contributes, giving about half the interior value (0.51).
points: Nearly uniform inside: field lines parallel and evenly spaced (the uniform-field criterion from Sec. 2 of the textbook).
Center 8128 μT, end 4156 μT (0.51 times), only 248 μT outside at 10.0 cm.
Inside, field lines run from S to N, so the thumb direction (+x end) is the N pole; outside it closely resembles a bar magnet.

en.q: Assessment: find the point on the solenoid where the reading is exactly half the interior value
en.concl: The assessment has no new conclusion: the half-value point is the end; "uniform inside, half at the end, like a bar magnet outside" come together on one device; strength is always judged by field-line density (textbook Exercise 6).
points: First fix the current at 2.0 A: B ∝ I, so changing the current changes the baseline.
Half of the center reading 8128 μT is 4156 μT.
When the reading falls to half, z = 6.0 cm, exactly at the end; beyond it the field decays rapidly.
